content: 1. Our confidence in the estimated effect is limited, and the true effect may differ significantly from the estimated effect. This is classified as low certainty. 2. When the certainty is very low, we have minimal confidence in the estimated effect, and the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimated effect. 3. The evidence was downgraded by one level due to the risk of bias. This includes unclear random sequence generation in three trials, unclear allocation concealment in six trials, unclear blinding of outcome assessment in three trials, incomplete outcome data in three trials, and a high risk of selective outcome reporting in one trial. 4. The evidence was downgraded by one level for inconsistency, as there were large variations in the effect and a lack of overlap among confidence intervals. 5. The evidence was downgraded by one level for imprecision due to very few events (fewer than 250). 6. The evidence was downgraded by one level for indirectness, as all trials were conducted in high-income countries, which may not be generalizable to other settings. 7. The evidence was downgraded by one level for risk of bias, including unclear allocation concealment in one trial and unclear blinding of outcome assessment in one trial. 8. The evidence was downgraded by one level for imprecision, as the confidence interval included no effects and there were very few study participants. 9. The evidence was downgraded by one level for indirectness, as all trials were conducted in high-income countries, limiting applicability to other contexts. 10. The evidence was downgraded to very low due to non-comparable results caused by differences in assessment methods used. 11. The evidence was downgraded by one level for risk of bias, including unclear allocation concealment and unclear blinding of outcome assessment. 12. The evidence was downgraded by two levels for imprecision. 13. Digital tracking of client information using mobile devices, combined with clinical decision support tools, may slightly increase the number of children under five receiving the Polio 3 vaccine. However, it likely makes little or no difference to the number of children fully immunized or receiving other vaccines such as BCG, DPT3, or measles. 14. This approach may increase the number of pregnant women taking at least 90 iron tablets during pregnancy and attending at least three antenatal care visits. However, it likely makes little or no difference to the number of women giving birth at healthcare facilities or receiving at least two tetanus injections. 15. The approach may increase the number of women initiating breastfeeding immediately after birth but likely makes little or no difference to the number of women exclusively breastfeeding for six months. 16. The approach may increase the number of women using contraception six months or later after giving birth but likely makes little or no difference to contraception use within six months postpartum. 17. There is very low certainty regarding the effect of this approach on emergency department visits among children with pulmonary disease, asthma severity during office visits, or hospitalizations among children with pulmonary disease. 18. There is very low certainty regarding the effect of this approach on providers' or patients' acceptability/satisfaction, time between presentation and appropriate management, quality of service data, providers' adherence to recommended practices, resource use, or unintended consequences. 19. Two studies assessed the effect of digital tracking combined with clinical decision support and targeted client communication. However, the evidence was of very low certainty, and no direct evidence was identified for the outcomes of interest. 20. No studies met the inclusion criteria for assessing the effect of digital tracking combined with targeted client communication alone. 21. Further high-quality trials are needed to robustly establish the effects of these multifaceted interventions delivered via mobile devices. 22. Digital tracking with clinical decision support compared to standard care in primary healthcare settings likely makes little or no difference to the number of children under five being fully immunized or receiving the BCG vaccine. 23. No studies were identified that reported on providers' adherence to recommended practices or the time between presentation and appropriate management. Therefore, the effect of this approach on these outcomes remains uncertain.
